lead: Don't just look at what happens right away; ask one more question: and then what?
when: When a decision looks like a great deal right now but might affect long-term habits, how work is shared on a team, or how other people behave, it's worth asking one more step.
body:
When you first come up with a fix, you often see only the most direct benefit: skip one check and you deliver faster today; handle all the hard problems for your coworkers and the trouble disappears right away. Second-order thinking asks us to look one step further. Once the check is skipped, will mistakes flow into the next stage? If you always finish things for others, will the same problems just come back next time?

Second-order thinking is a decision-analysis approach: beyond the direct results of an action, it traces the indirect effects those results cause, how other people respond, and the follow-on changes that unfold over time.

"Second-order" doesn't mean you may only think two steps ahead, and it isn't about who's smarter. It reminds us to connect the action, the direct result, and what follows, especially how others will respond and whether existing rules will change because of it. The same decision can also have different effects in the short term and the long term.

Take learning a new skill: at first you're slower and it's more tiring, but later you may be more independent and save time. Second-order thinking can show you the cost hidden behind an immediate benefit, and also the value that comes after an immediate struggle. It helps widen what you're comparing, rather than automatically rejecting fixes that work quickly.

When drawing it, put "what action you take" on the left, then connect "direct results" and "later effects." Where there are different possibilities, branch out; use dashed lines for links without enough evidence. The point isn't to draw long chains of arrows, but to spell out why each step might lead to the next.
example:
You lead a small team, and whenever someone hits a hard problem, you take it over and do it yourself. The first-order result is obvious: the task gets done quickly and the schedule stays on track. Keep asking "and then what?" and another possible path appears: your coworkers don't get a chance to practice and come back to you next time; you get busier and busier, and your own important work keeps getting pushed back.

That doesn't mean you should never help again. First judge whether it's urgent. If it has to be handled right away, finish it together. When there's time, have your coworker propose a plan first, then give hints, check the key steps, and ask them to finish it themselves. It may take a bit more time now, but it can cut the cost of taking things over again and again later.

This chain of changes is just a guess to be tested, not proof that helping once will make someone dependent. Try it on one common type of problem for two weeks, see whether your coworkers finish more on their own and whether you spend less time on that kind of problem, then adjust.
extra:
To sleep ten more minutes each day, you always leave packing tomorrow's things until right before you head out. You get a bit more sleep now, but what may follow is rushing to find things, forgetting documents, and having to go back for them. What you really need to compare is the time and energy of the whole morning, not just the moment you get up.

Try spending five minutes the night before getting things ready, and see after a week whether your mornings are less frantic. If packing ahead doesn't help, look for other causes. Factoring in later effects also means letting the facts correct what you first imagined.
steps: First write down the most direct benefits and costs of the decision, without skipping the immediate issues.
Then ask "and then what?" two more times: how will others respond, what new tasks or opportunities will come up, and which parts are uncertain?
Compare the short-term and later effects, pick a small approach you can adjust, and check your predictions against real feedback.
caution: Thinking far ahead doesn't make your predictions accurate. Each extra link can bring in new assumptions, so don't turn a chain of "maybes" into "definitely," and don't only imagine the worst case. Ordinary small things don't need endless analysis, and in an emergency, deal with the immediate risk first. Second-order thinking focuses on later effects, opportunity cost focuses on the alternatives you give up, and a feedback loop requires results to come back and affect the starting point. You can use all three together, but they aren't quite the same.
exercise: Pick a decision you're about to make and write three columns: "direct results," "what might happen next," and "who will change what they do because of it." Choose the item that affects the decision most and is least certain, and think about how you could check it first.
brief: Looking far down a chain reaction: a stick figure gets ready to gently push the first domino with one hand while watching what follows through a telescope; the first chain splits into two more distant possible paths, one driving gears and a seedling, the other affecting a block on a support. Off-white background, dark gray line art, navy arrows, small touches of brick red, no text.
diagramCaption: From left to right: taking over the task, finishing it now, and being asked for help again next time. The branches on the right show the possible added time pressure and fewer chances to practice. The dashed lines indicate these later effects still need to be checked.
